Integrating multimodal MRI and pathological correlation will be important for disentangling these components. Third, the present analyses primarily focused on global T1-WMHypo burden. Although additional regional and spatial analyses were performed, finer-grained compartmental modeling of WM may yield additional disease-specific insights and improve interpretability. Finally, the prognostic associations observed in only limited brain disorders, while encouraging, require external validation and prospective confirmation before clinical translation.

In summary, this study established age-and sex-specific normative references for T1-WMHypoV across the lifespan and demonstrated their applicability across a wide range of neurological and psychiatric disorders. By contextualizing individual T1-WMHypo burden within a normative framework, we show that this marker captures a dimension of WM pathophysiological changes partially independent of conventional T2-FLAIR hyperintensity. Normative deviation patterns vary substantially across diseases, contribute to disease diagnosis and relate to brain structural alterations, functional impairment, and clinical outcomes in various brain disorders. These findings highlight T1-WMHypoV deviations as an individualized imaging marker for characterizing WM pathophysiological characteristics and advancing precision approaches to brain development, aging and diseases.

Methods

Participants

Three-dimensional T1WI scans with isotropic voxel sizes of 1 mm or less were collected for a total of 41,735 scans. The dataset comprised 34,148 scans from HCs and 7,587 scans from individuals with neurological or psychiatric disorders. Detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria are provided as follows.

Inclusion criteria included (1) availability of high-quality three-dimensional T1-weighted MRI data, and (2) diagnoses established according to internationally reuse, remix, or adapt this material for any purpose without crediting the original authors. Exclusion criteria included a history of additional neurological or neuropsychiatric disorders, incomplete MRI acquisition, inadequate image quality, or unsuccessful image segmentation. Follow-up scans were excluded from cross-sectional analyses.

After quality control and exclusions, the final cohort comprised 34,148 HCs and 7,587 patients (details see Table 1). The distribution of participants across 146 centers is shown in Fig. 1a,b.

Age or date of birth was extracted from DICOM metadata or obtained directly from participants or their legal guardians. Available clinical variables included age, sex, and years of education (n=6,442). Cognitive assessments included MoCA (n=5,636) and MMSE (n=4,850). Additional cognitive measures were available in subsets of MS, NMOSD and MOGAD patients, including SDMT (n=950) and PASAT (n=926).

Motor and disability assessments were available for specific patient groups. Among PD patients, UPDRS-III assessments were obtained in the off-medication state (n=788), on-medication state (n=783), and after DBS (n=498). Baseline and follow-up EDSS scores were available for 850 MS and 394 NMOSD patients, respectively, for neuroinflammatory diseases. Mood assessment, including Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA, n=1,866) and Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD, n=1,873) were assessed for specific patient groups. Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (POSI, n=253) for a subset was also acquired.

MRI Acquisition and Image Processing

MRI data were obtained from 146 sites. All participants underwent three-dimensional T1WIs, typically using a magnetization-prepared rapid gradient echo sequence, with isotropic voxel sizes of 1 mm or less. A subset of participants additionally underwent T2-weighted FLAIR imaging. All images were independently reviewed for quality by two trained raters, with discrepancies resolved by consensus involving a third reviewer. T1WI data were processed using the FreeSurfer (version 7.3.2). Standard preprocessing steps included correction for intensity non-uniformity, skull stripping, intensity normalization, and registration to Talairach space. Volumetric measures were extracted from the aseg.stats and aparc.stats outputs, including WMV, cortical GMV, sGMV, cerebellar volume, brainstem volume, CSF volume, mean cortical thickness, total cortical surface area, and TIV. T1-WMHypoV was derived from intensity-based segmentation within the WM mask as implemented in FreeSurfer. All T1-WMHypo segmented images were spatially resampled and aligned to a standard template before regional analysis. WMH were parcellated into seven anatomical regions using the Hammers atlas: corpus callosum, basal ganglia, frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital and insula. For participants with available T2-weighted FLAIR images, T2-WMHyper segmentation was performed using a previously validated deep learning model (66). Quality control was conducted at multiple stages of the processing pipeline. Raw MRI scans were visually inspected for motion artifacts and acquisition-related abnormalities. Automated outlier detection was applied to segmentation outputs, and manual inspection was performed when necessary. To mitigate residual site-related variability, values exceeding three standard deviations from the site-specific mean were excluded from subsequent analyses.

Normative modeling

Normative lifespan models for T1-WMHypoV and other brain structure metrics were constructed using the HC cohort within the GAMLSS implemented in R (version 4.3).

Age and sex were included as fixed effects, and scanning site/center was modeled as a random effect. A generalized gamma distribution was selected to account for the right-skewed distribution of volume measures. Age-related effects were modeled using fractional polynomials, with model complexity determined by the Bayesian Information Criterion. To reduce potential bias in deviation estimation, 10-fold cross-validation was applied. Individualized centile scores were derived for each participant based on the normative models. All patient scans were acquired at sites represented in the normative dataset, allowing appropriate adjustment for site-related effects. Age-related rates of change were estimated by computing the first derivative of the fitted median trajectory across the lifespan.

Statistical analysis

All statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.3, R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Categorical variables are presented as counts (percentages) and were compared using Pearson's chi-square tests. Continuous variables are reported as means ± standard deviation and compared using one-way analysis of variance when approximately normally distributed, or as medians with interquartile ranges (or ranges) and compared using the Kruskal-Wallis test when distributions were non-normal.

Normative deviation scores of T1-WMHypoV and other structure metrics were calculated for all participants based on the age-and sex-specific normative reference models. Group-level differences in deviations T1-WMHypoV and other brain structure metrics between patients and HCs were assessed using Monte Carlo permutation tests with the Welch t statistic. When available, HCs were matched to patients by age, sex, and scanning site; otherwise, unmatched HCs were used. Effect sizes were quantified using Cohen's d with 95%CIs. Multiple comparisons across disease groups were controlled using the FDR procedure.

To assess whether the T1-WMHypoV has an additional contribution to the disease differential diagnosis, we performed a series of classifications among the above brain disorders using logistic regression. To test the potential contribution of T1-WMHypoV deviations, we compared the adjusted McFadden R² between full (all variates were considered) and reduced models (all variates except T1-WMHypoV reuse, remix, or adapt this material for any purpose without crediting the original authors.

A part of brain morphological imaging phenotype measures (example datasets approved by local centers) derived by FreeSurfer have been shared at GitHub (https://github.com/zhuozhizheng/T1-WMHypo-normative-references) and Science Data Bank (https://www.scidb.cn/s/yqy6Jb).

Main codes used for the statistical analyses and figures are publicly available at GitHub (https://github.com/zhuozhizheng/T1-WMHypo-normative-references) and Science Data Bank (https://www.scidb.cn/s/yqy6Jb).

Significant T1-WMHypoV deviations were observed in the majority of neurological disorders (11/17, 65%) and only major depressive disorder (MDD) in psychiatric disorders (1/4, 25%), with marked heterogeneity in effect magnitude. Large deviations (|d| ≥ 0.8) were detected in idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH, Cohen's d = -2.25, 95%CI [-2.62, -1.88], pFDR < 0.001), neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease (NIID, d = -1.65 [-2.13, -1.17], pFDR < 0.001), cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD, d = -1.26 [-1.37, -1.15], pFDR < 0.001), and MS (d = -0.85 [-1.09, -0.74], pFDR < 0.001). Moderate deviations (0.5 ≤ |d| < 0.8) were observed in Alzheimer's disease (AD, d = -0.74 [-0.87, -0.61], pFDR < 0.001) and progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP, d = -0.69 [-1.08, -0.30], pFDR < 0.001). Small yet statistically significant deviations (|d| ≥ 0.2) were detected in epilepsy (d = -0.48 [-0.86, -0.10], pFDR = 0.013), multiple system atrophy-Parkinsonian variant (MSA-P, d = -0.48 [-0.74, -0.21], pFDR < 0.001), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE, d = -0.46 [-0.84, -0.07], pFDR < 0.020), MDD (d = -0.45 [-0.58, -0.31], pFDR < 0.001), reuse, remix, or adapt this material for any purpose without crediting the original authors. this preprint (which was not certified by peer review) in the Public Domain. Significant negative correlations with Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA, r = -0.23 to -0.37) were observed in AD, iNPH, MSA-C and CSVD, as well as PSP (FDR-unsurvived) and MOGAD (FDR-unsurvived). Similar negative associations with Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE, r = -0.26 to -0.41) were observed in AD, iNPH, and CSVD, as well as PSP (FDR-unsurvived) and MSA-C (FDR-unsurvived). In addition, negative association with MMSE (r = -0.38) was observed in epilepsy (FDR-unsurvived) In MS and MOGAD (FDR-uncorrected), higher T1-WMHypoV was associated with lower Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT) performance (r = -0.29 and -0.32, respectively). In addition, T1-WMHypoV showed a negative correlation with Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test (PASAT) scores in MOGAD (r = -0.31, FDR-unsurvived). Univariate analyses and partial correlations with additional adjustment for T2-WMHyperV yielded comparable findings.White Matter Hypointensity Stratified Patients with Different Treatment Response and Disease ProgressionWe further examined the potential predictive ability of T1-WMHypoV for treatment response in PD, and disease progression in MS and NMOSD. For treatment response assessment in PD, we defined the PD cases with extreme deviations (centile score > 0.95) as the high T1-WMHypo burden subgroup, and the remaining as the low T1-WMHypo burden subgroup. Between-group differences in motor improvement after medication and one-year follow-up after deep brain stimulation (DBS) therapy were analyzed by Student's t-test. The same deviation cutoffs were also applied for MS and NMOSD cases to define the high and low T1-WMHypo burden subgroups.Kaplan-Meier analysis with a log-rank test was conducted to investigate the potential differences in disease progression (EDSS worsening in MS and NMOSD, and conversion to secondary progressive MS [SPMS] from relapsing-remitting MS [RRMS]) of the stratified subgroups. We additionally conducted multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression to test the independent predictive value of T1-WMHypoV deviations, by considering age, sex, and other brain structural metrics. In PD, patients with high T1-WMHypoV deviations showed more severe motor impairment than those with low deviations, reflected by higher Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale-Part III (UPDRS-III) scores both under medication and in the DBS-off state (both p < 0.001, Fig 2d). Patients in the high T1-WMHypoV subgroup demonstrated lower motor improvement in response to medication compared with those in the low T1-WMHypoV subgroup (p = 0.013). In contrast, no significant difference in motor improvement following DBS was observed between subgroups (p = 0.304), indicating that T1-WMHypoV burden is associated with pharmacological responsiveness but does not predict DBS-related benefit. reuse, remix, or adapt this material for any purpose without crediting the original authors. this preprint (which was not certified by peer review) in the Public Domain. Kaplan-Meier analyses demonstrated that the patients with high-deviation subgroup showed a greater risk of EDSS worsening (p < 0.001) and an increased risk of conversion from relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS, shortened as MS in the above contents) to SPMS (p < 0.001). At 5 years of follow-up, the cumulative probability of EDSS worsening was 38.91% [28.80%, 47.59%] in the high-deviation group compared with 22.73% [95%CI, 9.15%, 34.29%] in the low T1-WMHypoV group. The cumulative probability of SPMS conversion was 24.22% [14.37%, 32.95%] in the high-deviation group compared with 9.93% [0.00%, 18.89%] in the low T1-WMHypoV group. In NMOSD, stratification using the high-deviation threshold (centile > 0.95) did not reveal a significant difference in disability progression between subgroups (p = 0.157). However, when a lower threshold (centile > 0.50) was applied, patients with high T1-WMHypoV deviations showed a greater risk of EDSS worsening compared with those with low deviations (p = 0.004). At 5 years of follow-up, the cumulative probability of EDSS worsening was 65.08% [38.83%, 80.07%] in the high-deviation group compared with 20.39% [7.06%, 31.80%] in the low T1-WMHypoV group. Across demyelinating disorders, the prognostic relevance of T1-WMHypoV deviations was further supported by multivariate Cox regression analyses, in which higher T1-WMHypoV deviations remained associated with increased risk of disability progression after adjustment for demographic factors, and other brain structural metrics in MS (Extended Data Fig 3). Comparison of Normative Reference and Clinical Relevance with T2-WMHyperV across HCs and Brain Disorders Based on the available T2-WMHyperV (n=2,276 for HCs, and n=2,939 for brain disorders), we first analyzed the correlations between absolute raw T1-WMHyoV and T2-WMHyperV by univariate Pearson correlation across HC and disease groups. Then we fitted the normative reference of T2-WMHyperV with the same method as described in the T1-WMHypoV normative reference construction. The deviations of T2-WMHyperV across HCs and brain disorders were calculated and compared as described in the T1-WMHypoV deviation analysis. Univariate Pearson correlation with other brain structural metrics and clinical scores was conducted to test the clinical relevance of T2-WMHyperV deviations for comparison with those in T1-WMHypoV. Comparisons between T1-WMHypoV and T2-WMHyperV were performed in different conditions (in all cases and subsets with low T2-WMHyperV [volume < 1ml]).

Similar correlations with clinical scores were observed (negative r ranges from -0.47 to 0.22, positive correlation with MoCA in Younger-HC [r=0.30], all pFDR < 0.05) (Fig 4d) between T2-WMHyperV and T1-WMHypoV. For those cases with low T2-WMHyperV (volume < 1ml), the T1-WMHypo showed significant larger volume than T2-WMHyper (Fig 4f), indicating the predominant pathologies reflected by T1-WMHypo at low T2-WMHyper burden. Meanwhile in the low T2-WMHyperV cases, the T1-WMHypoV deviations largely preserved the correlations with other brain structural metrics and clinical scores (Fig 4g, h), which implied T1-WMHypo is a sensitive and clinically relevant marker of WM alterations at low or absent burden of T2-WMHyper.

Significant longitudinal increases in T1-WMHypoV were observed in MS (β = 0.32, 95% CI [0.09, 0.55], pFDR = 0.027) and NMOSD (β = 0.31, 95% CI [0.08, 0.54], pFDR = 0.027) over the disease course (Extended Data Fig 4). In contrast, no significant longitudinal changes were detected in MCI (β = 0.18, 95% CI [-0.13, 0.49], pFDR = 0.26), AD (β = 0.20, 95% CI [-0.06, 0.45], pFDR = 0.15), or CSVD (β = 0.20, 95% CI [0.00, 0.39], pFDR = 0.085), although the direction of effect in CSVD was positive.Then, we repeated the analyses of T1-WMHypoV burden across HCs and brain disorders by raw T1-WMHypoV as well as correlation analyses with other raw brain structural metrics and clinical scores (Extended Data Fig.5). The findings showed that the deviation score was more sensitive to reveal the T1-WMHypoV deviation in some brain disorders (e.g., PSP, MSA-P, Epilepsy and MDD). The deviation scores and raw values of T1-WMHypoV had comparable correlations with other brain tissue metrics and clinical scores, which further confirmed the findings by normative reference derived deviations.

Given this biological heterogeneity, interpreting the absolute burden of T1-WMHypo can be challenging, whereas normative modeling offers a principled approach for quantifying individual T1-WMHypo burden relative to population distributions. Using this framework, T1-WMHypoV exhibited a robust J-shaped trajectory across the lifespan, which was consistently observed across different WM regions, indicating a shared developmental and aging signature. The increasing limb of this trajectory in adulthood parallels this preprint (which was not certified by peer review) in the Public Domain.

[McFadden R² of full model -McFadden R² of reduced model]) and relative (defined as [McFadden R² of full model -McFadden R² of reduced model]/McFadden R² of reduced model*100%) changes of McFadden R², and the p values distribution of Likelihood Ratio Test across the paired classifications among brain disorders were reported. Associations between T1-WMHypoV deviations with brain structural metrics and clinical scores were examined using Pearson correlation analyses. Three complementary approaches were applied: univariate correlations, partial correlations adjusted for age, sex, and TIV, and partial correlations with additional adjustment for T2-WMHyperV to assess independence from conventional lesion burden. Brain structural metrics included T2-WMHyperV, WMV, cortical and sGMVs, cerebellar and brainstem volumes, CSF volume, mean cortical thickness, and total cortical surface area. Clinical scores comprised global cognitive scores, disability and motor assessments, and affective and sleep-related scales. Multiple comparisons were controlled using FDR correction across diagnostic groups and outcome measures. To evaluate the prognostic value of T1-WMHypoV deviations, analyses were conducted in PD, MS and NMOSD. For treatment response assessment in PD, we defined the PD cases with extreme deviations (centile score > 0.95) as the high T1-WMHypo burden subgroup, and the remaining as the low T1-WMHypo burden subgroup.
